tapinarof.summary: A prescription steroid-free cream that calms psoriasis and eczema plaques, leaving visible skin clearer and smoother.

quick.overview:
Tapinarof (Vtama) is a prescription cream that clears the visible red, scaly plaques of psoriasis and eczema, so skin looks clearer and smoother. It is steroid-free and approved in the US for plaque psoriasis in adults and atopic dermatitis in adults and children aged 2 and older.

It activates the aryl hydrocarbon receptor in skin cells, which lab studies link to less inflammation and better barrier proteins; the label says the exact mechanism is unknown. Two phase 3 trials in plaque psoriasis were published in 2021, and a phase 2b trial reported efficacy in atopic dermatitis. Seborrheic dermatitis is described as under study, with no trial found in the sources reviewed.
quick.how: It is a 1% cream applied to affected patches as directed by a prescriber, as an ongoing treatment for the skin condition rather than a cosmetic. People use it where plaques show, and results build over weeks of regular use.
quick.risks: Label-listed reactions in psoriasis include folliculitis, nasopharyngitis, contact dermatitis and headache. Human pregnancy data are insufficient. It is prescription only.

angle.text: Tapinarof clears the visible plaques and redness of psoriasis and eczema, leaving skin clearer and smoother. It works by activating the AhR receptor in skin cells, which lowers inflammation. Phase 3 trials support its psoriasis use.

roflumilast-cream.summary: A prescription steroid-free cream and foam that reduces redness and flaking from psoriasis, eczema and scalp or facial seborrheic dermatitis.

quick.overview:
Roflumilast (Zoryve) is a prescription cream and foam that clears the visible redness, scale and flaking of psoriasis, eczema and seborrheic dermatitis on the scalp and face. The FDA approved the 0.3% cream for plaque psoriasis in July 2022, the 0.3% foam for seborrheic dermatitis in December 2023, and a 0.15% cream for atopic dermatitis in July 2024.

It selectively inhibits phosphodiesterase-4, an enzyme involved in inflammatory signaling in skin, so inflammation and scaling settle and skin looks calmer. Phase 3 randomized trials have tested it in plaque psoriasis and atopic dermatitis. Uses such as vitiligo have no trials behind them in the sources reviewed.
quick.how: People apply the cream to plaques or the foam to scalp and facial areas as directed by a prescriber. It is steroid-free, used as ongoing treatment for the condition, with visible improvement building over weeks.
quick.risks: It is prescription only. Topical adverse events are reported in trial publications and on the label; oral roflumilast tablets list diarrhea, nausea, headache and insomnia.

angle.text: Roflumilast cream and foam clear the visible redness, scale and flaking of psoriasis, eczema and scalp or facial seborrheic dermatitis. It blocks PDE-4 to lower skin inflammation, so scalp and face look clearer. Phase 3 trials cover psoriasis and eczema.

sofpironium.summary: A prescription underarm gel that cuts excessive sweating, keeping shirts dry and free of visible sweat marks.

quick.overview:
Sofpironium is a prescription gel applied to the underarms to reduce excessive sweating, so clothing stays dry and free of visible sweat marks. It was first approved in Japan in September 2020 as Ecclock and is sold in the US as Sofdra for primary axillary hyperhidrosis in adults and children aged 9 and older.

It blocks M3 muscarinic receptors on sweat glands where it is applied, reducing the signal that triggers sweating. Randomized trials have compared the gel with an inactive vehicle gel. It is a medicine for a recognised medical condition rather than a cosmetic.
quick.how: It is applied to the underarms as directed by a prescriber, as a daily-use topical. People use it for dry shirts and fewer sweat stains, and it only affects the area where it is applied.
quick.risks: Label-listed adverse reactions include dry mouth, blurred vision, dilated pupils, skin irritation and urinary retention. The label also warns about lack of sweating in hot conditions. It is prescription only.

angle.text: Sofpironium gel stops underarm sweat at the source, so shirts stay dry and sweat marks do not show. It blocks receptors on sweat glands where it is applied. It is a prescription medicine, approved in Japan as Ecclock and in the US as Sofdra, with randomized trial support.

dexpanthenol.summary: A vitamin B5 derivative in moisturizers and ointments that hydrates and calms dry or irritated skin so it looks smoother.

quick.overview:
Dexpanthenol (panthenol, provitamin B5) is a common moisturizer and ointment ingredient used to keep dry or irritated skin hydrated and calm, so it looks smoother and less flaky. It appears in barrier-supporting skincare, often at a few percent.

It is converted to pantothenic acid, part of coenzyme A that supports normal epithelial function, and acts as a humectant that draws water into the skin. It penetrates well and reaches high local concentrations. Research, including a 70th-anniversary review and a 2020 wound-healing review, has centred on wound healing, skin irritation and radiation-related skin reactions, mostly in small trials.
quick.how: People use it in creams, lotions and ointments applied to dry, chapped or irritated areas, often as part of a barrier-repair routine. Hydration shows up soon after application, while repair of irritated skin takes days.
quick.risks: Topical use is described as well tolerated in the reviews listed. This entry does not cover injected B-vitamin products.

angle.text: Dexpanthenol draws moisture into skin and supports the barrier, so dry, irritated skin looks smoother and calmer. It is a vitamin B5 derivative studied mainly for wound healing and skin irritation.

calendula-extract.summary: Marigold flower extract in soothing skincare, used to calm irritated, red-looking skin; studied for wound healing.

quick.overview:
Calendula extract comes from pot marigold flowers and is used in creams and balms to calm irritated skin so it looks less red and more comfortable. It has a long history in traditional wound-care products.

Laboratory studies report anti-inflammatory activity for flower extracts, though the mechanism in human skin is not established in the sources reviewed. A 2019 systematic review of calendula as a single wound-healing treatment covered 14 studies, 7 in animals and 7 clinical trials. No published trial listed here has tested it for appearance goals such as acne or skin aging.
quick.how: People use it in soothing creams, balms and toners applied to irritated or sensitive skin, usually as part of a gentle routine. It is typically one ingredient among several.
quick.risks: The sources reviewed do not describe significant adverse effects of topical use; safety data are limited to the small studies cited.

angle.text: Calendula extract is used to calm irritated skin so it looks less red and more even. Lab studies report anti-inflammatory activity, and human and animal studies have looked at wound healing.

ciclopirox-shampoo.summary: A prescription antifungal shampoo that clears scalp flaking and redness from seborrheic dermatitis for a cleaner, flake-free scalp.

quick.overview:
Ciclopirox shampoo is a medicated antifungal wash used to clear the flaking, redness and itching of seborrheic dermatitis, the inflamed scalp condition that overlaps with dandruff. The payoff is a cleaner, flake-free scalp and hair. It is prescription-only in the US.

Ciclopirox is a hydroxypyridone antifungal active against Malassezia yeasts and described as having anti-inflammatory properties; its mechanism differs from the azoles and is not fully understood. Randomized trials have tested the 1% shampoo against vehicle for scalp seborrheic dermatitis and as an adjunct in childhood tinea capitis. No trial found tested it for hair growth.
quick.how: People use it as a regular medicated wash, often alternating with or alongside ketoconazole shampoo in hair-loss and scalp-care circles. Flaking typically improves over a few weeks of repeated use.
quick.risks: Systemic absorption from topical use is reported to be low. It is a prescription medicine in the US and Canada; local irritation is the usual concern with medicated shampoos.

angle.text: Ciclopirox shampoo targets the Malassezia yeast behind scalp flaking and redness, leaving a cleaner, flake-free scalp and hair. Several vehicle-controlled trials cover seborrheic dermatitis; none have examined hair growth.

climbazole.summary: An azole antifungal in anti-dandruff shampoos and conditioners that reduces visible flaking and itching.

quick.overview:
Climbazole is an azole antifungal added to over-the-counter dandruff shampoos, lotions and conditioners, sometimes alongside zinc pyrithione, to cut visible flaking and itching for a cleaner scalp. It targets the Malassezia yeasts thought to contribute to dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis.

It belongs to the same class as ketoconazole and is described as inhibiting the fungal enzyme CYP51, which blocks ergosterol production in fungal membranes. Most published research concerns its presence in wastewater, rivers and fish. A 2001 clinical study of a climbazole shampoo for seborrheic scalp eczema is cited by Wikipedia, though no trial details were available.
quick.how: People use it as part of a regular anti-dandruff shampoo or conditioner routine, left on the scalp briefly before rinsing. It is bought over the counter, often as one active among several.
quick.risks: Local irritation such as redness and itching is reported. Grokipedia describes cosmetic-use limits in the EU and a 2024 ECHA flag for possible endocrine-disrupting properties; it is also reported as toxic to aquatic life.

angle.text: Climbazole is an antifungal in anti-dandruff products that goes after the yeast behind scalp flaking, so hair and shoulders look cleaner. It is in the same azole class as ketoconazole; the research in the sources is mostly environmental.

coal-tar-shampoo.summary: An old-school over-the-counter tar shampoo that clears flaking and scaling from dandruff, seborrheic dermatitis and scalp psoriasis.

quick.overview:
Coal tar shampoo is an over-the-counter medicated wash used to clear the flakes and scale of dandruff, seborrheic dermatitis and scalp psoriasis, leaving a clearer scalp with fewer visible flakes. Coal tar is a dark by-product of coke and coal-gas production.

Tar is traditionally described as keratolytic and anti-inflammatory, slowing scalp skin turnover, though Wikipedia does not detail how it works. Controlled studies from 1980 to 2000 reported it effective in psoriasis, dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis, while a double-blind trial found a non-tar shampoo as effective as a 0.5% coal tar shampoo for dandruff.
quick.how: People use it as a medicated wash a few times a week, lathered on the scalp and left briefly before rinsing. Its strong smell and staining limit how many stick with it.
quick.risks: Irritation, folliculitis, phototoxicity and contact dermatitis are reported. Coal tars are IARC Group 1 carcinogens, and a mid-1990s Lancet correspondence debated carcinogenic potential and measured skin uptake after hair washing. Wikipedia reports the EU forbade coal tar in cosmetics in 2009.

angle.text: Coal tar shampoo slows scalp skin turnover to clear flaking and scaling from dandruff and scalp psoriasis, so the scalp looks clearer. Controlled studies reported it effective; its odor and staining limit acceptance.

glycerin.summary: The common humectant in moisturizers, cleansers and shaving products that keeps skin hydrated, soft and smooth-looking.

quick.overview:
Glycerin is a thick, sweet, water-attracting liquid found in most moisturizers, soaps and many hair and shaving products. It keeps skin hydrated and gives it a smoother, softer, plumper look and feel.

It is hygroscopic, so it draws in and holds water, which is why it works as a humectant. Beyond cosmetics it is used as a laxative in suppositories, a tablet and syrup excipient, and a food additive (E422). The sources reviewed contain no randomized trial of glycerin as a cosmetic moisturizer; registered trials study other uses such as suppositories.
quick.how: People get it as an ingredient in daily moisturizers, cleansers and shaving products, applied to damp skin. Hydration is felt right after application.
quick.risks: Oral toxicity is described as very low, though large amounts can affect children. Past diethylene glycol contamination caused deaths, leading to FDA batch-testing advice in 2007.

angle.text: Glycerin pulls water into the skin surface and holds it there, so skin looks softer, smoother and more hydrated. It is among the most common ingredients in skin care, with long use documented.

lanolin.summary: A wool-derived emollient wax in lip balms and moisturizers that softens dry, chapped skin and lips.

quick.overview:
Lanolin is a waxy substance from sheep wool, refined into an emollient for lip balms, moisturizers, baby care and nipple creams. It softens dry, chapped skin and lips so they look smoother and less cracked.

Its sterol and wax esters resemble lipids in human skin; it forms an occlusive layer that seals in moisture and can take up water. It is described as long-lasting at holding moisture. Registered trials compare it with other topicals for sore nipples in breastfeeding women, and Wikipedia states evidence for a soothing effect is limited. No cosmetic trials were found.
quick.how: People apply it as a lip balm or rich moisturizer on dry patches, often overnight. Purified, low-pesticide grades are standardized in the US and European pharmacopoeias.
quick.risks: It is a relatively common contact allergen, though Wikipedia says its sensitizing potential was historically overstated. Purified grades are sold as low-allergen.

angle.text: Lanolin seals moisture into dry skin and lips, leaving them softer and less chapped. It resembles the lipids in human skin; trials have focused mainly on sore nipples rather than facial appearance.

dimethicone.summary: A silicone oil in primers, moisturizers and hair products that leaves a smooth film, softening fine lines and pores and adding shine.

quick.overview:
Dimethicone is a silicone oil in primers, moisturizers, shampoos, conditioners and hair serums. It leaves a smooth, silky film that visibly softens the look of fine lines and pores and adds slip and shine to hair. The smoothing is visible as soon as it is applied.

It is a long-chain silicone polymer that is hydrophobic and optically clear, forming a thin water-repellent layer on skin or hair. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel concluded it is safe as used in cosmetics. Published human trials concern medical uses such as incontinence-associated dermatitis and head lice, not long-term appearance outcomes.
quick.how: People meet it in the base of makeup primers, moisturizers and leave-in hair products, applied under makeup or on hair lengths. The effect lasts while the film stays on and washes off with cleansing.
quick.risks: Silicone granulomas reported in the literature arise from injected liquid silicone, not topical use. It is not biodegradable but is removed in wastewater treatment.

angle.text: Dimethicone leaves a smooth, silky film on skin and hair, visibly softening fine lines and pores and adding shine on application. Trials cover medical skin-protectant uses rather than long-term appearance outcomes.

shea-butter.summary: A rich plant fat from African shea nuts used as a moisturizer for dry skin, lips and hair ends, leaving them softer and less flaky.

quick.overview:
Shea butter is a creamy fat from the nuts of the African shea tree (Vitellaria paradoxa), used as a rich moisturizer for dry skin, lips and hair ends so they look softer and less flaky. It is also used in soaps, hair products and, in some regions, cooking.

It is mainly a triglyceride fat rich in oleic and stearic acids that coats and softens the skin as an emollient. Traditional use for dry skin, burns and rashes is documented, and lab studies have examined anti-inflammatory triterpenes in its unsaponifiable fraction. Small trials have tested shea-containing products; none found tests shea butter alone for appearance.
quick.how: People apply it directly or in creams and balms to dry areas, lips and hair ends, often at night. Unrefined butter is popular for its fuller content.
quick.risks: Safety assessments cited by Grokipedia describe low toxicity for skin and oral use. Highly refined grades are reported to retain much less of the vitamin and phenolic content than raw butter.

angle.text: Shea butter coats and seals dry skin with fatty acids, so skin, lips and hair ends look softer and less flaky. It rests on long traditional use and lab composition data.

sodium-pca.summary: A humectant salt that occurs in skin's natural moisturizing factor, used in moisturizers and toners for plumper, less dry-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Sodium PCA is a humectant in moisturizers, toners and hair products that keeps skin hydrated so it looks plumper and less dry. It is the sodium salt of pyroglutamic acid, a compound skin makes naturally as part of its natural moisturizing factor.

As a humectant it binds water at the surface. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review Expert Panel reassessed PCA and its salts as skin-conditioning humectants. It is rarely studied on its own and mostly appears as one ingredient within formulations, so evidence is mostly its safety review and its role in skin biology.
quick.how: People get it as an ingredient in daily moisturizers, toners and hair products rather than as a standalone product. Surface hydration is felt on application.
quick.risks: Wikipedia describes it as low in toxicity and not a skin irritant.

angle.text: Sodium PCA binds water at the skin surface, so skin looks plumper and less dry. It is a salt of a compound naturally found in the skin's moisturizing factor.

sodium-lactate.summary: A lactic acid salt in moisturizers, shampoos and soaps that holds water and balances pH for softer-feeling skin.

quick.overview:
Sodium lactate is a mild salt of lactic acid used in shampoos, liquid soaps and some moisturizers to hold water and balance pH, helping skin feel softer and smoother. It is the salt of lactic acid, a familiar exfoliating acid.

As a humectant it attracts and holds water, and as a salt of a weak acid it buffers pH. It is also a food preservative (E325) and part of hospital fluids such as Ringer's lactate. Its medical roles are better documented than its appearance effects, and no trials were found testing it for appearance.
quick.how: People meet it as a listed ingredient in everyday cleansers and moisturizers rather than as a product of its own. It is made by fermenting a sugar source and neutralising the resulting lactic acid.
quick.risks: In topical and food use it is generally regarded as low-risk by the sources reviewed. Intravenous use is medical, is contraindicated in lactic acidosis, and can induce panic attacks in people with panic disorder.

angle.text: Sodium lactate helps skin hold water and keeps product pH in range, so skin feels softer and smoother. It is the salt of lactic acid; its medical uses are better documented than its appearance effects.

trehalose.summary: A protective sugar in some moisturizers and serums that binds water and shields cells, with autophagy interest in anti-aging circles.

quick.overview:
Trehalose is a sugar that many organisms use to survive drying and stress. It is added to some moisturizers and serums as a water-binding, protective ingredient for hydrated, healthier-looking skin, and is discussed in anti-aging circles for its link to autophagy.

It stabilises proteins and membranes during dehydration. In mammalian cells it has been reported to trigger autophagy, partly through the TFEB pathway, though the mechanism is debated. Those findings come largely from cell and animal models of neurodegeneration, and small human trials are registered. No study found tests it for appearance.
quick.how: People encounter it in foods, dry-eye drops and cosmetic products where it is listed as a moisturizing ingredient. In skincare it is applied topically as part of a hydrating routine.
quick.risks: It is broken down to glucose by trehalase and is generally treated as safe in foods. Trehalase deficiency is uncommon, and a link to C. difficile outbreaks was disputed by a 2019 study.

angle.text: Trehalose binds water and protects cells from drying stress, so skin looks more hydrated and healthier. Its autophagy findings come from lab and animal research.

polyglutamic-acid.summary: A fermentation-derived humectant polymer in serums and essences that binds water for a plump, dewy look.

quick.overview:
Polyglutamic acid is a long chain of glutamic acid made by Bacillus bacteria and found in the Japanese food natto. Skincare brands use it in serums and essences as a water-holding ingredient for a plump, dewy look, and some marketing says it holds more water than hyaluronic acid.

The polymer is water-soluble and carries many negative charges, which lets it bind water. It is listed as a cosmeceutical ingredient. Its best-documented human trials involve alpha-PGA as a carrier in the chemotherapy conjugate paclitaxel poliglumex. No trials found test it for skin appearance, and the comparison with hyaluronic acid comes from AI-generated or marketing sources without cited trials.
quick.how: People use it in lightweight serums and essences layered under moisturizer, usually combined with other humectants. Hydration is visible on application.
quick.risks: Gamma-PGA is described as biodegradable and non-immunogenic. Wikipedia notes its medical use is largely pre-clinical, and safety data for topical cosmetic use were not found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Polyglutamic acid binds large amounts of water at the skin surface, giving a plumper, dewier look. Its established clinical use is as a drug carrier; appearance claims rest mainly on lab comparisons and brand testing.

propanediol.summary: A glycol humectant and solvent in the base of serums and moisturizers that hydrates and helps other actives dissolve and spread.

quick.overview:
Propanediol is a small two-hydroxyl molecule used in serums, moisturizers and makeup to hydrate skin, improve texture and help other ingredients dissolve and spread. Two forms are used: 1,2-propanediol (propylene glycol) and 1,3-propanediol, often made by fermentation and sold as a plant-derived alternative.

As a humectant it binds water, and as a solvent and penetration enhancer it helps other ingredients dissolve and move into the upper skin layers, according to encyclopedic descriptions. It is a supporting ingredient in the base of products rather than a treatment, and no human trial has tested it as a standalone appearance treatment.
quick.how: People get it as part of the base of serums, moisturizers and makeup rather than on its own. It often lets actives feel lighter and spread more evenly.
quick.risks: Toxicity is described as low, but contact allergy is reported in an estimated 0.8 to 3.5 percent of people depending on concentration. Propylene glycol was the American Contact Dermatitis Society's 2018 Allergen of the Year.

angle.text: Propanediol hydrates skin and helps other actives dissolve, absorb and spread, giving a smoother-feeling, better-delivered skincare routine. It is chosen as a plant-derived alternative to propylene glycol.

ectoin.summary: A bacteria-derived protective molecule in barrier and soothing skincare, used for hydration, less redness and UV-stress protection.

quick.overview:
Ectoin (ectoine) is a small molecule that salt-loving bacteria make to survive harsh conditions. Skincare brands put it in moisturisers and sun-care products to hydrate, calm redness and protect skin from UV and pollution stress, for calmer, more even-looking skin.

It is a compatible solute that organises water around proteins and membranes and stabilises them. A 2004 study in cultured skin cells reported it reduced several markers of UVA-induced damage. A registered trial has examined a 7 percent ectoin cream for hydration and barrier function in atopic dermatitis, and other ectoin products have been studied for airway, nasal and eye conditions. No published trial has tested it for facial appearance in healthy people.
quick.how: People use it in barrier-support creams, soothing serums and daytime sun-care as part of a calming routine. It is often paired with other hydrating ingredients.
quick.risks: The sources reviewed describe it as well tolerated in nasal-spray use and report no specific skin safety concerns; formal safety data for cosmetic use are limited.

angle.text: Ectoin protects cells from stress and supports the barrier, so skin looks calmer, better hydrated and less red. Lab data on UV stress exist.

beta-glucan.summary: An oat or yeast polysaccharide in creams and serums that hydrates and soothes, so skin looks calmer and less dry.

quick.overview:
Beta-glucans are sugar polymers from oats, barley, yeast and fungi. In skincare, oat and yeast forms appear in creams and serums to hydrate and soothe, so skin looks calmer, less red and less dry.

Cosmetic descriptions cite water-binding and film-forming properties. Most research concerns other roles: oat beta-glucan is a soluble fibre for which the US FDA approved a heart-disease risk claim in 1997 relating to LDL cholesterol, and immune cells recognise beta-glucans through dectin-1 and related receptors. No clinical trial in the sources reviewed tested topical beta-glucan for appearance.
quick.how: People use it in soothing creams, serums and masks, often oat or yeast based, applied to dry or irritated skin as part of a calming routine.
quick.risks: Oral forms are widely eaten as fibre. The sources reviewed list no specific topical safety signals, and also provide no topical safety trials.

angle.text: Beta-glucan forms a hydrating film on skin, so it looks calmer, less red and less dry. It is well studied as dietary fibre and an immune trigger, while topical appearance use has not been trialled in the sources reviewed.

allantoin.summary: A classic soothing additive in drugstore moisturizers, lip balms and scar products that softens rough skin and calms irritation.

quick.overview:
Allantoin is a gentle, widely used ingredient in moisturisers, scar gels, lip products, after-shave and sun care. Brands position it to soften rough skin, soothe irritation and leave skin smoother and calmer-looking.

Cosmetic sources describe it as a humectant that attracts water, with mild anti-inflammatory and antioxidant action. It is a nitrogen compound formed when uric acid is oxidised; most mammals make it enzymatically, humans do not, and cosmetic grade is generally synthetic. Studies exist for scar and wound products that contain it, but they combine it with other ingredients, so its own effect is not isolated.
quick.how: People get it in everyday drugstore products and scar and wound formulas, applied to rough, irritated or healing skin. It is almost always one ingredient among several.
quick.risks: Wikipedia describes it as safe and non-toxic in cosmetic use, with a rat oral LD50 above 5,000 mg per kg.

angle.text: Allantoin softens the skin surface and calms irritation, so rough skin looks smoother and calmer. It is a long-standing drugstore additive, also used in scar and wound combination products.
